    The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (480 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months.
    • Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months.
    • Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

    Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

    Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

    Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

    They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

    The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

    Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

    The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

    The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

    Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

    Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

    By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

    The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

    The water group also indicated greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

    Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

    It has been revealed that dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, remarked:.

    “It’s a small change with the potential for a massive impact on long-term health outcomes.”.

    The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

    In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

    However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

    The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

    The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

    They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

    The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

    In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

    Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

    Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

    The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

    Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

    Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

    After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

    One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

    Industry observers note that “Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

    Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

    Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

    The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

    When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

    A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

    Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

    A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

    The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.
    • One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.
    • Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

    One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

    Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

    Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

    Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

    Short skirts highlighted almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

    Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

    Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

    Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

    White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

    These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

    The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

    They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

    Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

    The results showed that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

    For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

    The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

    “That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

    The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

    2 Personality Traits Are Linked to Lower Inflammation

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (497 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.
    • Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.
    • People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

    Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

    People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.

    Among the qualities that make up conscientiousness, being hardworking and organised stood out.

    For extraversion, which includes both sociability and energy, the clearest result was for people who described themselves as active.

    These patterns matter because inflammation that stays elevated over time is linked to both physical and psychological health.

    Lower levels of long-term inflammation are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, stroke and premature death.

    They have also been associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

    The researchers pooled data from six studies involving more than 19,000 adults in the United States, England and Japan.

    Participants rated how well words such as ‘organised’, ‘hardworking’ and ‘active’ described them.

    The researchers then looked at how those answers related to two markers of inflammation in blood samples, C-reactive protein and interleukin-6.

    Earlier research had already linked higher conscientiousness with lower levels of both inflammatory markers (Luchetti et al., 2014).

    In this study, people who described themselves as organised or hardworking tended to have lower levels of both markers.

    Being hardworking revealed the strongest association within conscientiousness, even stronger than the association for the overall trait score.

    People who scored higher on extraversion tended to have lower C-reactive protein, and much of that association came from how active they said they were.

    In fact, being active was more strongly associated with lower C-reactive protein than any other characteristic the researchers examined.

    Being talkative showed a small association in the opposite direction, while being lively was associated with lower levels of both inflammatory markers.

    In several of the studies, the association with being active held up even after the researchers took other aspects of extraversion into account.

    Being active and hardworking may both reflect how much energy people have for everyday tasks.

    In earlier research, people who scored higher on the activity aspect of extraversion or the achievement-striving aspect of conscientiousness tended to have better aerobic capacity during a brisk walking test (Terracciano et al., 2013).

    Regular physical activity could help explain part of the association with inflammation.

    The relationship could run in the other direction, too, if people with higher inflammation feel less energetic and come to see themselves as less active or lively.

    The study was published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology (Stephan et al., 2026).

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry?
    • It has been revealed that energy, mood or sleep lost to worry?
    • Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

    It has been revealed that energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

    Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

    Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

    Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

    The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

    They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

    On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

    The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

    The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

    Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

    Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

    Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

    Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

    The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

    Breaking: Two Everyday Drink Swaps Are Linked To Less Weight Gain

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
    • Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
    • Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

    Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

    Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

    Replacing them with diet drinks shows much the same pattern.

    Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

    Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

    A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

    The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

    The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

    Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

    The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

    The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

    People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

    The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

    Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

    Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

    In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones indicated a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

    That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

    The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).

    Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
    • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
    • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

    Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

    People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

    Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

    Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

    They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

    Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

    The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

    Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

    Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

    One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

    If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

    Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

    By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

    Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, said:.

    “These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

    When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

    A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

    The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

    The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

    The Positive Personality Trait Linked To Having A Crush Outside Your Relationship

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
    • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
    • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

    What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

    Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

    The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

    Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

    The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a new attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

    People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

    The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

    They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

    The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

    Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

    People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

    Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

    The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone new.

    Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, revealed a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

    People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

    Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also highlighted a reversal.

    It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

    The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

    Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

    When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

    Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

    The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

    #35608. The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (589 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Org ↗ Open Full Page

    The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
    • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
    • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

    The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

    Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

    These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

    For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

    Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

    In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

    Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

    In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

    Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

    Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

    Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

    Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

    The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

    Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

    They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

    About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

    The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

    The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

    A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

    Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

    The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

    A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

    For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

    The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.
    • The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.
    • Children and teenagers who report frequent or severe headaches tend to have lower vitamin D levels.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

    The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

    Children and teenagers who report frequent or severe headaches tend to have lower vitamin D levels.

    The link was modest overall but stronger among girls and among teenagers.

    Body mass index, or BMI, accounted for about a fifth of the association in the researchers’ statistical model.

    One possibility is that vitamin D and body weight are both related to inflammation, which can affect how sensitive the nervous system is to pain.

    Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

    The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

    The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

    The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

    Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

    Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

    The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

    Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

    For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

    Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

    The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

    The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).

    #35604. This Vitamin Deficiency May Double Heart Disease Risk

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (545 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Org ↗ Open Full Page

    This Vitamin Deficiency May Double Heart Disease Risk

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.
    • People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.
    • A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

    People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

    A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

    After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

    Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

    A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

    In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

    The results highlighted that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

    Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

    Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

    The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

    To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

    They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

    Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

    The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

    Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, said:.

    “Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very vital to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

    For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

    Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

    “We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

    This said, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

    If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

    Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially key, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

    Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

    In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

    The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).
